transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-01-20 11:57 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-01-20T10:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 59.542 degrees and its azimuth is 151.107 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 47.814 degrees and its azimuth is 124.404 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 2.74 percent illuminated, 19.022 degrees from the Sun, and 385267.8 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest with you: **No, you will not be able to see the Moon with your unaided eyes right now.**

While your app correctly shows that the Moon is physically "above the horizon," there are three major factors working against you in this specific scenario:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout"
You mentioned the Sun's altitude is **59.542 degrees**. This means the Sun is very high in the sky, creating intense, direct sunlight. In "bright daylight" conditions, the atmosphere is flooded with scattered sunlight (Rayleigh scattering). This creates a high level of background luminance that completely overwhelms the relatively dim light reflected by a crescent Moon.

### 2. The Moon's Phase (The "Crescent" Problem)
The Moon is only **2.74% illuminated**. This is a very thin, "waxing crescent." Because it is so close to the Sun (only 19 degrees away), it is positioned in the brightest part of the sky. 
*   **The Rule of Thumb:** To see a crescent Moon during the day, it usually needs to be much further from the Sun (lower in the sky, closer to the horizon) where the atmosphere can help dim the surrounding blue sky, or it needs to be much larger (closer to a Full Moon).

### 3. Contrast
Visibility is all about contrast. Because the Moon is currently positioned in the same general area of the sky as the Sun (Azimuth 124° vs 151°), it is sitting in the "glare" zone. Even if the Moon were a Full Moon, it would be incredibly difficult to see at this time of day; at only 2.74% illumination, it is effectively invisible against the blue of the daytime sky.

**The Verdict:**
If you look toward the coordinates provided, you will see a very bright, clear blue sky. The Moon is there, but it is being "drowned out" by the sheer volume of sunlight. 

**When to try again:**
To see this specific Moon, you'll want to wait until **dusk**. As the Sun sets and the ambient light of the sky drops, that thin crescent will begin to "pop" against the darkening blue.
